    About

    What this site is

    Zero Divisors presents a mathematical physics research programme written in the language of Clifford’s geometric algebra. This is the algebra of directions, in which directions can be multiplied and in which the number systems of physics become parts of a single algebra.

    At its core are new theorems about division by zero (e.g. by a null vector). Where an element has no inverse, the theorems treat it not as a dead end but as a signpost to a larger algebra in which the division can be carried out. These theorems are then applied to gravitational singularities, to quantum theory, and to the particles and forces of the Standard Model. The work lands on many known theories and results, whilst offering a fresh perspective and new ideas.

    The Physics Graph holds every result once: its statement, its proof, what it rests on, and, where it has one, the machine check that verifies it. Follow any result down through everything beneath it. Humans can explore it visually, and AI agents can navigate it through a set of tools (Explore with AI). Your own AI can evaluate the project for itself, for example where the mathematics is strongest and where the physics is speculative, and you can ask it further questions to dig deeper.

    The graph is open source: anyone can propose a new result or a correction through a pull request. Each pull request is checked before it is accepted, and the result is credited to its author. Qualified physicists and mathematicians are able to endorse or challenge individual results under their own name, each review signed through ORCID so that it cannot be altered or quietly removed.

    New here? The Introductions are three short, illustrated presentations for a general audience.

    How the work came to be

    At the heart of the framework is Leon Butler’s proposal that where division by zero fails in a Clifford algebra, the failure is not a dead end but an instruction: the space is carried into a higher-dimensional algebra in which the division takes a value, without a multiplicative inverse ever appearing. The mathematics was developed in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic’s AI system. An extended session with Claude Fable 5 over the summer of 2026 produced the first draft of a monograph, Zero Divisors as Signposts.

    The monograph was iterated upon until it became too unwieldy to verify as a single document. It was therefore split into the Transport Papers (T0 to T17) and two guides. At this point the work became far more rigorous: each paper carries a script that checks its results in exact arithmetic, and results proved in a paper are kept apart from those taken from the literature. The AI largely performed the proofs and drafting; Leon directed the work, spot-checked it and stepped in when the reasoning drifted. The models were the most capable publicly available in the summer of 2026, and far stronger at sustained mathematics than those of two years earlier. The papers are on Zenodo as preprints and have not yet been through journal peer review.

    How the work was checked

    The guide, G00 (The Transport Papers: A Guide, in the Transport Papers community on Zenodo), explains how the series fits together and how it was checked. Each paper went back and forth between an AI model that wrote it and a separate AI model that attacked it, until the review found nothing further or a finding was declined with its reason recorded. Every paper ships with a script that tests its results in exact rational arithmetic, so each check either passes exactly or fails; together, the research papers’ scripts run more than sixteen hundred checks. The core statements of the root paper, T1, are also proved in the Lean 4 proof assistant. Proved results are kept apart from literature results, which are labelled as imported facts with their source. The guide meets the same standard: every reference resolves against the papers, no claim is stated more strongly than the paper that proves it, and withdrawn claims are blocked from reappearing.

    A script shows that the named identities hold and the quoted numbers recompute. It cannot show that a proof is sound or the physics right. That is the job of human review.

    Why a graph

    A series of papers has the monograph’s problem on a larger scale: a result used in several papers must be updated in each one by hand. The Physics Graph solves this. Each result is held once, with its statement, proof, dependencies and check, and the site’s versions of the papers are generated from the graph, so a correction reaches every document that uses it.

    The graph was designed in collaboration with the AI, in the form it found easiest to navigate: separate results linked to what they rest on, read through tools rather than by searching long documents. That same design opens it to others, whether or not they work with an AI of their own.

    By design and where possible, all theorems and proofs are written in geometric algebra. The graph therefore also consolidates the physics it covers into one mathematical framework.

    Leon Butler holds a BSc (Hons) in Mathematics from the University of Manchester.
